newsitem.title: UK: British election will not stall EU talks - Dutch.
newsitem.headline: British election will not stall EU talks - Dutch.

text.p: European Union talks on the bloc's future development cannot be put on hold until Britain's general election is out of the way, Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo said on Wednesday.

Speaking on his first visit to Britain since his country took over as president of the EU, he told journalists: "We are not looking at the coming months as a period of just waiting until the British elections have taken place."
The Dutch, who hold the EU presidency for the first half of this year, hope to wrap up the bloc's Intergovernmental Conference with a summit meeting in Amsterdam in June.

The Conference has been discussing reforms to the way decisions are taken in the EU, but the British Conservative government has been resisting any moves to give more power to Brussels or to dilute its right of veto.

This has prompted speculation that other EU countries were delaying key decisions in the hope that a British election due by May would result in the election of a more pliant British government under opposition Labour leader Tony Blair.
But Van Mierlo said although discussions would finish after a British election, they could not be held up by its imminence.
He was speaking in Britain's Foreign Office alongside foreign minister Malcolm Rifkind before the two men held talks.

Rifkind said the British government would be happy to see the EU accept the principle of "flexibility" under which groups of member states willing to integrate faster than others were allowed to do so.

France, Germany and other EU states have suggested that "flexibility" could be used to get round the reluctance of some EU countries such as Britain to move as quickly towards closer integration as others want to.

But Rifkind said Britain would resist any suggestion that EU institutions such as the executive Commission could be involved in a programme of cooperation between some EU states that was not approved by all the others.
"EU institutions belong to all 15 member countries...the principle of acceptability to all 15 is fundamental," he said.
